source.title: Cognitive motor processes: the role of motor imagery in the study of motor representations.

confidence_rationale: A review of motor-imagery evidence for Jeannerod's mental-simulation theory: imagined, observed and executed actions share core motor representations (including primary motor cortex activation during imagery) and differ chiefly in whether execution is gated. This is genuinely mixed evidence for Q-068 -- the shared-representation finding argues that simulated/intended/acted are NOT separate machinery (favouring the MECH-094 write-profile view, where one representation written under different profiles suffices), while the systematic behavioural/temporal differences between imagery and execution argue the statuses are nonetheless distinguishable. Confidence moderate: a synthesis review, and its imagery-vs-execution axis covers only part of the five-way vocabulary.
failure_signatures: If simulated and executed actions required wholly separate representations, the consistent overlap (including M1 activation and matched mental/actual movement durations) reported here would not occur -- so a design that hard-separates every action-status into independent machinery would over-fragment what is biologically one core representation differentiated by gating.

Conversely, the measurable mental-vs-actual timing and performance differences mean a model that treats simulation and execution as identical (no status distinction at all) would also be wrong; the review does not specify how many discrete statuses are warranted.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Behavioural, fMRI and TMS evidence supports mental-simulation theory: motor imagery, action observation and motor execution share the same motor representations -- motor areas including primary motor cortex are active during imagery, and mental performance durations closely match actual durations -- with the principal difference being that overt execution is gated/inhibited during imagery.
mapping.ree_translation: Bearing on Q-068's core tension: if simulated, intended and executed actions are one shared representation differentiated mainly by an execution gate, then REE's MECH-094 simulation/commit write-profiles plus the MECH-061 commit-boundary token (which is essentially an execution-gate marker on a shared representation) may already carry the distinction without a separate first-class status vocabulary. The shared-representation evidence thus partly weakens the case for an explicit graded vocabulary, while the reliably measurable imagery-vs-execution differences keep the distinction real -- supporting that the statuses exist but can be read off gating rather than stored as independent annotations.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The review's axis is imagery vs observation vs execution; it does not separately treat rehearsed vs intended vs committed, nor self_reference_frame, so it informs the simulated/acted endpoints of Q-068 but not the middle distinctions. 'Shared representation' is a claim about overlap, not identity -- it does not prove write-profiles are sufficient, only that a single-core-plus-gating account is biologically plausible.
mapping.source_context: Human cognitive-neuroscience review; motor imagery behavioural studies, fMRI and TMS.

confidence_components.notes: Solid synthesis review directly on the simulated-vs-executed question, but only the endpoints of Q-068's gradient; the mixed direction is intrinsic to the evidence, not a weakness of the source.
